summary: The note traces the history of a local Senior Olympics, from its late-20th-century origins under Dr. William Morgan through decades of growth, highlighting standout athletes in each era. It anticipates the 2023 opening ceremonies on September 3 and stresses the games' value for community, health, and intergenerational connection, framing aging as continued striving rather than diminishment.
one_line: A decade-by-decade history of a community Senior Olympics, its standout older athletes, and its impact on health, community and generations, ahead of the September 3, 2023 opening.
key_facts: The opening ceremonies of the Senior Olympics are set for September 3, 2023.
Dr. William Morgan, an advocate for senior fitness, orchestrated the initial concept; the first local games had just a handful of athletes.
In the 1980s, Nancy Thompson, a 47-year-old runner, became an icon who challenged aging stereotypes and inspired more senior athletes to compete.
In the 1990s, Jack Robertson, 65, was remembered for his stunning display in the shot put.
In the 1990s, cities across the country began recognizing such events, and new sports were added to accommodate diverse skills and interests.
In the 2000s, technology allowed for more refined training methods and record-keeping.
Gracie Martinez, a 70-year-old table tennis enthusiast, became a viral sensation in the 2000s.
In the 2010s, Edward "Fast Eddie" Clarkson, age 80, outran competitors half his age.
For the current edition, Marjorie Harris, a renowned 75-year-old swimmer, is slated to compete again.
George Fernandez, age 82, aims to defend his senior cycling crown.
Doctors and nutritionists frequently cite the games as a reference point, encouraging patients to stay active.
The note says the games have an intergenerational impact, with grandchildren watching grandparents compete.
